data.text:
[00:00:00–00:00:20] professor: Good morning. Today we move from estimation to hypothesis testing, which is the second half of inference.
[00:00:21–00:00:47] professor: Last week we built confidence intervals. A test asks a sharper question: is the data compatible with one specific value?
[00:00:48–00:01:13] professor: We always start from two statements. The null hypothesis, H zero, and the alternative, H one.
[00:01:14–00:01:42] professor: The null is the boring claim. For example, the mean waiting time at the clinic is twenty minutes.
[00:01:43–00:02:16] professor: The alternative is what we would believe if the evidence is strong enough. Say, the mean is longer than twenty minutes.
[00:02:17–00:02:48] professor: Notice the asymmetry. We never prove the null. We either reject it, or we fail to reject it.
[00:02:49–00:03:33] professor: Now, the test statistic. For a mean with known sigma, we use z equals x bar minus mu zero, over sigma divided by root n.
[00:03:34–00:04:00] professor: Under the null, this statistic follows a standard normal distribution. That is the whole trick.
[00:04:01–00:04:42] professor: Let us do the example on the slide. Sample of thirty-six patients, sample mean twenty-two point five minutes, sigma six.
[00:04:43–00:05:08] professor: So z is two point five divided by one, which gives two point five.
[00:05:09–00:05:55] professor: Is two point five large? We compare it with the critical value. At the five percent level, one-sided, the critical value is one point six four five.
[00:05:56–00:06:30] professor: Two point five is beyond one point six four five, so we reject the null hypothesis at the five percent level.
[00:06:31–00:07:11] professor: The p-value says the same thing in a different language. It is the probability, under the null, of a result at least this extreme.
[00:07:12–00:07:46] professor: Here the p-value is about zero point zero zero six. Small p-value, strong evidence against the null.
[00:07:47–00:08:25] professor: A very common mistake in the exam: the p-value is not the probability that the null is true. Please do not write that.
[00:08:26–00:09:07] professor: Two kinds of error. Type one error: we reject a true null. Its probability is alpha, the significance level we choose.
[00:09:08–00:09:49] professor: Type two error: we fail to reject a false null. Its probability is beta, and one minus beta is the power of the test.
[00:09:50–00:10:25] professor: There is a trade-off. If you make alpha smaller, beta grows, unless you collect a larger sample.
[00:10:26–00:11:07] professor: Two-sided tests split alpha in the two tails. At five percent, the critical values become plus and minus one point nine six.
[00:11:08–00:11:51] professor: When sigma is unknown, we replace it with the sample standard deviation and use the t distribution with n minus one degrees of freedom.
[00:11:52–00:12:18] professor: The logic does not change. Only the table you read the critical value from.
[00:12:19–00:13:00] professor: For next week, do exercises four to nine in problem set four. Exercise seven is the kind of question I like for the exam.
[00:13:01–00:13:45] professor: Any questions? Yes. Can we use the confidence interval to run the test? Good question, and yes, for a two-sided test they agree.
[00:13:46–00:14:26] professor: If the hypothesized value falls outside the ninety-five percent interval, you reject at the five percent level. Same decision.
